items.title: Johnny DeDroit Interview, 1969-12-04
items.q: But Dutch Andrews helped me get the collection.

ctx.x: What is his name? Wyatt Sharp.

W-Y-A-T-T-S-H-A-R-P. I didn't know him. He played with me at Suburban Gardens, and he was a very bright man. He managed by hook or crook, by leaving his clothes in his locker after Suburban Gardens, that he slept two nights in the Roosevelt and paid for one. Yeah, that's the truth. Because he was on the Donbusters, you see. He played with Pinky on the Donbusters. So he'd move in and leave a call for Donbusters, six o'clock, and he'd move out. Because most of his clothes and his tucks were in the locker at the…
You think the band wasn't any good when you bid $350?

items.title: Johnny DeDroit Interview, 1973-03-16
items.q: Because he had people who played well but were not like Dutch Andrews, who I think is a fine trumpet player. Dutch can't read. I tried to use him and he couldn't read.

ctx.x: Talking about style, on your other interview you mentioned arguing with the Captain Strykfuss about the kind of music you'd play on the boat. He said something about he wanted you to play like what he'd heard in St. Louis, and he says you're in New Orleans and you play like what people in New Orleans wanted. How would you contrast the two? What would be the…

I didn't contrast them because I didn't know what they played in St. Louis. But to give me a list of ten best tunes in St. Louis that some of them I'd never heard of, but didn't know how they played out. I just said, Captain, I play New Orleans music. And I don't think that the people in New Orleans want to sing most music. I said, I don't know what it is. And then he said to me, he said, well you're working against me. I said, Captain, I'm not working against you. I said, with all due respect to you, you're a…
ever been there? And you're always playing Dixieland
